subject: Cooking
title: Spinach Isn't Actually High in Iron
description: A short lesson to help you apply Spinach Isn't Actually High in Iron.

hook.text: Popeye ate spinach for iron-powered strength. But spinach's iron reputation is built on a decimal point error.

buildup.text: In 1870, German chemist Erich von Wolf recorded spinach's iron content as 35mg per 100g — ten times too high.

discovery.text: The real figure is 3.5mg — comparable to many other vegetables. A misplaced decimal created the myth.

twist.text: Spinach also contains oxalic acid, which binds to iron and prevents absorption — making its iron even less useful.

climax.text: The error wasn't corrected until 1937. By then, Popeye had already cemented spinach's iron reputation forever.

punchline.text: A typo in 1870 created a cartoon character's entire identity.

quiz.question: What caused the myth that spinach is exceptionally high in iron?
options: A decimal point error in an 1870 scientific paper

details.summary: Spinach contains moderate iron, not the exceptional levels that Popeye popularized. The myth may have originated from a decimal point error in 19th-century research that overstated spinach's iron content tenfold. Additionally, spinach's oxalates block most of its iron from being absorbed.
details.whyItMatters: This myth elevated spinach above genuinely iron-rich foods like red meat and lentils. Understanding bioavailability — how much iron your body actually absorbs — matters more than total iron content.
takeaways: The original iron measurement may have had a decimal point error
Oxalates in spinach bind iron, reducing absorption significantly
Red meat, lentils, and fortified cereals provide more usable iron

faq.question: How much iron does spinach actually provide?
faq.answer: Raw spinach contains about 2.7 mg of iron per 100 grams, which is moderate but not exceptional. More importantly, only about 2 to 5 percent of that iron is absorbed due to oxalate binding. The same serving of beef provides iron with 15 to 35 percent absorption.

faq.question: Was the decimal point error story true?
faq.answer: The story that a German chemist misplaced a decimal in 1870 is widely told but debated by historians. Whether or not the specific error occurred, spinach's iron content was genuinely overstated in popular culture. Popeye cartoons from the 1930s cemented the exaggeration.
